text: In Haiti and its diaspora, Haitians and Haitian Americans commonly practice Voodoo, speak Creole, and express their cultural identity through dance and music as a means of cultural expression and preservation. This behavior is aimed at maintaining a strong sense of cultural identity within the community, while the recipient, society, and Haitian Americans engage in cultural assimilation and the sharing of language, religion, and culture. The influence of French culture, language proficiency, and the resulting isolation play a significant role in shaping these behaviors. This cultural practice is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, reflecting the importance of cultural preservation and expression among Haitians and Haitian Americans.

In Haiti and its diaspora, Haitian people and the government are often observed struggling with poverty, corruption, and social issues while striving for power and independence. Their goal encompasses survival, economic development, and social advancement amidst complex societal and political dynamics. In response, the international community and compatriots provide aid and experience societal influence within this context. The historical backdrop of slavery, revolution, and international isolation significantly influences these dynamics. This behavior is considered to be controversial and not widely regarded as the standard within the sampled population, reflecting the challenging and multifaceted nature of the societal and political dynamics in Haiti and its diaspora.

In Haitian culture, it is common for people to use cloves in cooking, often employing unique methods such as using the whole bag and various preparation techniques. This practice is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population.

Haitians tend to be v ery indirect in communicating . O ften times points are made with stories and parables as many people take the long way around to get to the point. A good conversation starter is to talk or ask about one’s family. Humor and laughter play a big role in communicating. It’s best to avoid talking about politics until you have established a strong relationship with someone. Conversation via telephone is commonplace, but it is no substitute for personal visits and conversation in person.

Haitians tend to prefer standing about an arm’s length from one another while conversing. This space may be less between goof friends and family. There is usually a fair amount of touching between men and men, and women and women and men and women while conversing. Light touching on the arms , hands , and shoulders is common. It is common to see people holding hands in public but kissing or hugging in a romantic sense is not usually appropriate.

Haitians tend to favor direct eye contact over indirect. During conversations direct eye contact is commonplace rather than sporadic as it shows a sign of interest and respect towards the speaker. Staring is not usually considered rude, especially if people are looking at foreigners. Be prepared to be stared at non stop.

In it is very common for people to have to wait for services, appointments, etc. Most accept it as a norm and give freely of their time regardless of the situation. Punctuality is not highly valued and being late is usually not considered rude. Transportation services like the “tap-tap” ( taxi/bus combo), do not tend to run on time and will usually depart when they are full.

Gender roles tend to follow the traditional route throughout the country. Women usually do all laundry, cooking, cleaning, child rearing , etc. and the men work the fields (rural areas) or other jobs (urban areas).
Whistling at someone is considered rude, as is p ointing.
The legal drinking age is 16, and is not readily enforced. Penalties for possession, acquisition, and trafficking of drugs are severe and include mandatory lengthy imprisonment in local jails.
It's best to ask permission before taking pictures of locals .

For Men - nice pants, dress shirt and tie . P ants are a MUST in gov ernmen t and business offices . S horts are not allowed. Dress tends to be more casual in rural areas vs. urban. For Women - skirts or sometimes a more western pant suit is acceptable. Dress tends to be more casual in rural areas vs. urban. Being clean and well groomed is highly valued.

Titles are very important and it is best to address people directly by using their professional title or Mr., Mrs., or Miss, followed by the surname. It is advisable, although not required, to have one side of your business card translated into French. There is no specific ritual surrounding the giving of business cards although it is advisable to treat the card with respect.

When it comes to negotiating, most Haitians love the drama and show of negotiating. T he y may pretend to be horribly offended by your offer , but this is usually just a ploy to up the ante. Usually the best actor wins.
Lecture and r ote m emorization are the most common forms of teaching.
